newsitem.title: CHINA: Power struggle stymies China securities law.
newsitem.headline: Power struggle stymies China securities law.

text.p: A power struggle over who will control China's lucrative securities industry is holding up publication of a long-awaited securities law and ensuring no change in its share quota system, brokers said on Tuesday.

They said there was no sign of a compromise between the People's Bank of China and the Securities Commission under the State Council (cabinet) over the legislation that could set out objective criteria to decide which companies can issue stock.

"There is agreement on most of the content of the law after four years of discussion," said a Chinese broker. "But there is no agreement over who should regulate the industry, which is perceived as very profitable."

John Crossman, Shanghai representative of Jardine Fleming, said that the best solution would be a compromise, giving the People's Bank, the central bank, control over financial issues and the Securities Commission control over listing and other securities issues.
"But the battle is for all the chips," he said. "The battle is still going on."

The debate pits the central bank against the Securities Commission, which consists of representatives of major ministries and commissions and oversees the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), responsible for day-to-day running of the securities industry.
While the battle goes on, share issues will continue to be decided by a quota system which some brokers think is outdated and should be abandoned.

In 1993 and 1995 Beijing issued two share quotas totalling 10.5 billion yuan that were distributed to provinces, major cities and industrial bureaux, with companies fighting for the right to issue shares.
By September 10, 133 firms had issued 4.084 billion yuan of the second quota of 5.5 billion yuan which was announced in 1995, official figures show.
Companies seeking a listing apply to provincial securities authorities. If approved, the applications are submitted to the CSRC in Beijing which grants final approval.
The approval procedure is in the hands of officials and subject to pressure by national and regional politicians who lobby fiercely to have their favoured companies listed.

"Quotas in many sectors of the economy have shrunk or been eliminated," said a second Chinese broker. "If we want to have a free market, we must get rid of the quota system for shares and let the exchanges decide which firms can list.

"The government uses stock issues to channel money largely to state companies and rarely to foreign-owned ventures, private or collective firms that are the engine of China's economic growth," he said.
Crossman said the securities law could outline a list of criteria which firms seeking a listing would have to meet.
Brokerages would then select and sponsor companies and propose them for listing to the CSRC which would simply say yes or no, he said.
"But they do not want to give the list of criteria," he said. "If they did, they would lose control of the process."
